claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets do not arise solely from constituent count.
Differences in short-range order contribute to the mechanical-property differences among these alloys.
Local lattice distortions contribute to the mechanical-property differences among these alloys.
Short-range order and local lattice distortions modify dislocation mobility during deformation.
Short-range order and local lattice distortions modify twinning activity during deformation.
The compared alloys are equiatomic, single-phase FCC materials produced by identical thermomechanical processing.
Systematically removing one or more elements from the quinary alloy while retaining an FCC phase provides a controlled quinary–quaternary–ternary comparison.
The samples should have similar grain sizes and defect densities and be tested at identical strain rate and temperature.
Differences in chemical complexity produce variations in short-range order and local lattice distortion.
The quinary alloy has greater local lattice distortion than the lower-order alloys because of its enhanced chemical complexity.
The quinary alloy forms more short-range order than the lower-order alloys because of its enhanced chemical complexity.
Short-range order and local lattice distortion act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Short-range order and local lattice distortion promote deformation-induced twinning.
The proposed changes in dislocation motion and twinning synergistically increase both strength and ductility in the quinary alloy relative to lower-order alloys.
Under identical deformation conditions, the quinary alloy will have higher yield strength than its quaternary and ternary counterparts.
Under identical deformation conditions, the quinary alloy will have greater ductility than its quaternary and ternary counterparts.
Under identical deformation conditions, the quinary alloy will develop a greater density of deformation twins than its quaternary and ternary counterparts.
The hypothesis is intended to apply only to single-phase FCC alloys with similar grain sizes and processing histories.
Differences in grain size, processing history, or phase stability may confound interpretation of the comparison.
Failure of the quinary alloy to show statistically higher strength, ductility, and twin density correlated with greater measurable short-range order would falsify the proposed explanation.
